steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on learning regression models from disjoint annotations, where each annotator labels a different subset of the data. Explain the annotation-cost and annotator-bias problem, what is missing in prior work on crowd-sourced labels, and summarize our contrastive approach and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Large labeled datasets are costly; multiple annotators disagree
- Disjoint subsets per annotator as a cheaper alternative
- Prior work on noisy / crowd-sourced labels; gap for regression
- Our approach: Disjoint Contrastive Regression (DCR)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Costly datasets, annotator disagreement
  - large labeled datasets needed: object retrieval, tracking, crowd counting, multi-modal learning (cite each)
  - annotation very time-consuming, expensive
  - multiple annotators; individual preferences -> inconsistent labels, esp. qualitative/subjective tasks
  - usual fix: several annotators per sample + average/majority vote -> even heavier cost
- Disjoint subsets
  - more efficient: assign disjoint subsets to individual annotators
  - challenge: inconsistency and bias among annotators
- Prior work + gap
  - approaches for noisy labels / labeling bias from crowd-sourced annotations (cite)
  - many advances recently, esp. classification with crowd-sourced labels (cite)
  - regression: besides inter-annotator inconsistency, intra-annotator consistency: rankings from same annotator align with latent ground truth rankings (Fig. 1)
  - handling both for regression underexplored
- Our approach
  - disjoint margin ranking loss + gradient reversal layer (GRL) (cite)
  - extend margin ranking loss for disjoint annotations, using intra-annotator consistency + inter-annotator inconsistency -> robust embedding
  - regularize batch distribution to avoid collapse to naive solutions
  - GRL for annotator invariant representations
  - together: Disjoint Contrastive Regression (DCR); framework in Fig. 2
- Contributions
  - contrastive learning framework for regression with disjoint annotations
  - extended margin ranking loss for intra-/inter-annotator issues
  - GRL for annotator invariant embeddings
  - experiments: facial expression prediction, image quality assessment

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models need large-scale labeled datasets to boost their performance, for tasks such as object retrieval, tracking, crowd counting, and multi-modal learning. These datasets usually need a lot of annotation, which is very time-consuming and expensive. Also, a large-scale dataset is usually labeled by multiple annotators. Because of individual preferences, the labels are not always consistent between different annotators, especially for qualitative and subjective tasks. So to reduce annotator bias, each sample often has to be labeled by multiple annotators, and then an average or a majority vote is used to get the final labels, which makes the annotation cost even heavier. To reduce the labeling effort, it is more efficient to give disjoint subsets of the data to individual annotators to label. So the hard task becomes how to deal with the inconsistency and bias between different annotators.

Some approaches deal with the noisy-label problem or labeling biases from crowd-sourced annotations. There have been many advances in recent years, especially for classification tasks with crowd-sourced labels. For regression tasks, though, besides the inconsistency between multiple annotators, the consistency within one annotator also has to be considered: the rankings of samples labeled by the same annotator usually align well with the rankings of the latent ground truth scores. Fig. 1 shows an example of this. How to take into account both intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency for regression tasks is still underexplored.

- Our approach
  - disjoint margin ranking loss + gradient reversal layer (GRL) (cite)
  - extended margin ranking loss using intra-annotator consistency + inter-annotator inconsistency -> robust embedding
  - batch distribution regularization against collapse to naive solutions
  - GRL for annotator invariant representations
  - Disjoint Contrastive Regression (DCR), Fig. 2
- Contributions
  - contrastive framework for regression with disjoint annotations; extended margin ranking loss; GRL; experiments on facial expression prediction + image quality assessment

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning models need large-scale labeled datasets to boost their performance, for tasks such as object retrieval, tracking, crowd counting, and multi-modal learning. These datasets usually need a lot of annotation, which is very time-consuming and expensive. Also, a large-scale dataset is usually labeled by multiple annotators. Because of individual preferences, the labels are not always consistent between different annotators, especially for qualitative and subjective tasks. So to reduce annotator bias, each sample often has to be labeled by multiple annotators, and then an average or a majority vote is used to get the final labels, which makes the annotation cost even heavier. To reduce the labeling effort, it is more efficient to give disjoint subsets of the data to individual annotators to label. So the hard task becomes how to deal with the inconsistency and bias between different annotators.

Some approaches deal with the noisy-label problem or labeling biases from crowd-sourced annotations. There have been many advances in recent years, especially for classification tasks with crowd-sourced labels. For regression tasks, though, besides the inconsistency between multiple annotators, the consistency within one annotator also has to be considered: the rankings of samples labeled by the same annotator usually align well with the rankings of the latent ground truth scores. Fig. 1 shows an example of this. How to take into account both intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency for regression tasks is still underexplored.

In this paper, we present a new approach for regression tasks from disjoint annotations, using a disjoint margin ranking loss that we design and a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Specifically, we extend the margin ranking loss based on the facts of disjoint annotations, using both the intra-annotator consistency and the inter-annotator inconsistency, which gives a robust embedding framework. Besides that, we use regularization of the batch distribution so that it does not collapse to naive solutions. GRL is also used in model training to learn annotator invariant representations. All of these together make up our proposed framework, Disjoint Contrastive Regression (DCR). Fig. 2 shows the framework. The main contributions of this paper are:

- • We present a new contrastive learning framework for regression tasks with disjoint annotations.

- • We extend the margin ranking loss and deal with the intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency.

- • We use GRL in model training to learn annotator invariant embeddings.

- • We run experiments on the facial expression prediction task and the image quality assessment task, which show that the proposed DCR is effective.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale labeled datasets are in heavy demand to boost the performance of deep learning models, for tasks such as object retrieval [1], tracking [2], crowd counting [3], and multi-modal learning [4]. Such datasets often require costly annotation, which is extremely time-consuming and expensive. Moreover, a large-scale dataset is usually labeled by multiple annotators. Due to individual preferences, the labels are not always consistent among different annotators, especially for qualitative and subjective tasks. As a result, to reduce annotator bias, each sample is often labeled by multiple annotators, followed by an average or a majority vote to obtain the final labels, which leads to an even heavier annotation cost. To alleviate the labeling effort, it is more efficient to assign disjoint subsets of the data to individual annotators. Therefore, addressing the inconsistency and bias among different annotators becomes a tough task.

Some approaches [5,6,7,8,9,10] deal with the noisy-label issue or labeling biases from crowd-sourced annotations, and many advances [11,12,13,14] have been made in recent years, especially for classification tasks with crowd-sourced labels. For regression tasks, in addition to the inconsistency among multiple annotators, intra-annotator consistency also needs to be considered: the rankings of samples labeled by the same annotator usually align well with the rankings of the latent ground truth scores. An example of this phenomenon is shown in Fig. 1. How to account for both intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency in regression tasks is still underexplored.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for regression tasks from disjoint annotations with a designed disjoint margin ranking loss and a gradient reversal layer (GRL) [15]. Specifically, we extend the margin ranking loss based on the facts of disjoint annotations, adopting both intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency, which leads to a robust embedding framework. Besides that, regularization of the batch distribution is employed to avoid collapse to naive solutions, and GRL is further adopted in model training to learn annotator invariant representations. Together these make up our proposed framework, Disjoint Contrastive Regression (DCR), shown in Fig. 2. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

- • We present a novel contrastive learning framework for regression tasks with disjoint annotations.

- • We extend the margin ranking loss and resolve the intra-annotator consistency and inter-annotator inconsistency.

- • We adopt GRL in model training to learn annotator invariant embeddings.

- • We conduct experiments on the facial expression prediction task and the image quality assessment task, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed DCR.
